Count and exclude licenses with missing names or implausible age estimates, then prepare one row per estimated dog from the 2024 NYC licenses.

## Packages and helpers
```{r}
#| label: dog-preparation-setup
library(tidyverse)
source("helpers.R")
```

## Read the license records
Read ZIP codes as text because they are identifiers. Let `read_csv()` infer the other column types: birth and extract years become numbers, and license dates become date-times. `read_csv()` normally reads empty fields and the text "NA" as missing values and trims surrounding spaces. We count and exclude the remaining missing-name labels below.

Keep ZIP strings as supplied. Geographic matching belongs to the later income work.

```{r}
#| label: read-license-records
dogs_raw <- read_csv(
  "data/raw/nyc-dogs-2024.csv",
  col_types = cols(zipcode = col_character())
)

dogs_raw |>
  preview()
```

## Number the source records
Number the licenses before filtering or sorting. `source_row_id` lets us find each recorded license in the saved CSV after later transformations. `row_number()` assigns 1, 2, 3 and so on in the current row order.

```{r}
#| label: number-source-records
dogs_raw |>
  mutate(source_row_id = row_number()) ->
  licenses_numbered

licenses_numbered |>
  preview()
```

## Give the license fields clear names
Give the city's columns clear working names. This changes the headings without changing their values.

```{r}
#| label: name-license-columns
licenses_numbered |>
  rename(
    name = animalname,
    sex = animalgender,
    birth_year = animalbirth,
    breed = breedname,
    license_issue_date = licenseissueddate,
    license_expiry_date = licenseexpireddate
  ) ->
  licenses_renamed

licenses_renamed |>
  preview()
```

## Count missing names by ZIP
The city uses six text labels when a name is not recorded. Import has already read "NA" and empty fields as missing values; the other labels remain text. Count both kinds together: `is.na(name)` identifies existing missing values, and `name %in% missing_name_labels` identifies names in our exclusion list. The `|` means either condition is enough. `sum()` counts those records without adding a flag column or changing their names.

Group by the recorded ZIP to count all source licenses and the licenses without usable names, then divide to get the missing-name share. This shows whether some areas have less complete name information.

```{r}
#| label: summarize-missingness-by-zip
missing_name_labels <- c(
  "UNKNOWN", "NAME NOT PROVIDED", "NONE", "NA", ".", "NONAME"
)

licenses_renamed |>
  group_by(zipcode) |>
  summarise(
    source_license_records = n(),
    missing_name_records = sum(is.na(name) | name %in% missing_name_labels)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    missing_name_share = missing_name_records / source_license_records
  ) ->
  missing_by_zip

missing_by_zip |>
  filter(missing_name_records > 0) |>
  arrange(desc(missing_name_share)) |>
  preview()
```

The preview shows the six ZIPs with the largest missing-name shares; `missing_by_zip` retains every ZIP, including those with no missing names.

## Exclude licenses without names
`drop_na(name)` removes existing missing values. The following filter removes names in the exclusion list. `!` means "not": keep a name only when it is not one of those labels. No recoding is needed.

```{r}
#| label: exclude-missing-names
licenses_renamed |>
  drop_na(name) |>
  filter(!name %in% missing_name_labels) ->
  named_licenses

named_licenses |>
  preview()
```

## Count and exclude implausible ages

Estimate age when the license was issued by subtracting the recorded birth year from the issue year. Because we do not know the birthday, this is the age the dog turns that calendar year, not its exact age on the issue date. Keeping estimates from 0 through 25 is a judgment call, not a biological maximum; it may exclude genuine exceptionally old dogs.

`year()` extracts the year from the imported license date. It comes from lubridate, included in tidyverse. The birth year is already numeric, so subtract it directly. In this snapshot, the malformed birth years also produce ages outside the accepted range, so no separate four-digit check is needed. `between()` includes both endpoints.

The optional [birth-year inference reference](appendices/birth-year-inferences.qmd) preserves six considered corrections. We exclude those records rather than guess their birth years.

```{r}
#| label: exclude-unusable-birth-years
named_licenses |>
  mutate(issue_year = year(license_issue_date)) |>
  mutate(age_at_issue = issue_year - birth_year) ->
  licenses_with_age

licenses_with_age |>
  filter(!between(age_at_issue, 0, 25)) ->
  excluded_birth_year_licenses

excluded_birth_year_licenses |>
  count(birth_year, age_at_issue, name = "source_license_records", sort = TRUE) ->
  birth_year_exclusion_counts

birth_year_exclusion_counts

licenses_with_age |>
  filter(between(age_at_issue, 0, 25)) |>
  select(-issue_year, -age_at_issue) ->
  usable_licenses

usable_licenses |>
  preview()
```

This excludes 59 named licenses: 33 with malformed birth years and 26 with age estimates above 25 from four-digit birth years. Together with the 5,810 missing-name exclusions, it leaves 100,105 licenses for preparation.

## Record compound names and unknown breeds

Count these details in the cleaning report without excluding the dogs. Record compound names before removing spaces and hyphens. All unknown breeds in this snapshot are written as `Unknown`, so compare directly with that value.

The pattern below has two alternatives separated by `|`: whitespace between non-whitespace characters, or a hyphen with a non-whitespace, non-hyphen character on each side. It flags `MARY JANE` and `WALL-E`, but not a trailing hyphen such as `CHLOE-`. `str_detect()` returns TRUE when a name matches the pattern. Both report columns are left out of the final dog table.

```{r}
#| label: prepare-cleaning-report-fields
internal_name_separator <- "\\S\\s+\\S|[^\\s-]-[^\\s-]"

usable_licenses |>
  mutate(
    compound_name = str_detect(name, internal_name_separator),
    breed_unknown = breed == "Unknown"
  ) ->
  licenses_for_formatting

# These examples show an internal space, an internal hyphen and a trailing hyphen.
example_dog_names <- c("LADY SMITH", "WALL-E", "CHLOE-")

licenses_for_formatting |>
  filter(name %in% example_dog_names) |>
  distinct(name, compound_name)
```

## Format names for matching

Uppercase the whole name, then remove all whitespace and ASCII hyphens, including trailing hyphens. For example, `WALL-E` becomes `WALLE` and `CHLOE-` becomes `CHLOE`. The compound-name report counts internal separators; it does not control which hyphens are removed.

```{r}
#| label: format-names
licenses_for_formatting |>
  mutate(name = str_to_upper(name)) |>
  mutate(name = str_remove_all(name, "[\\s-]")) ->
  licenses_with_matching_names

# Compare the selected recorded names with their actual formatted values.
licenses_for_formatting |>
  filter(name %in% example_dog_names) |>
  select(source_row_id, recorded_name = name) ->
  name_formatting_examples

name_formatting_examples |>
  left_join(licenses_with_matching_names, by = "source_row_id") |>
  distinct(recorded_name, name)
```

The display joins each selected source row to that same row after formatting. A left join keeps every selected example; `source_row_id` identifies the corresponding license. `distinct()` shows each before-and-after spelling once. This comparison is only a display and does not change the preparation tables.

## Consolidate repeated licenses and likely renewals

We estimate dogs from license records, without a dog identifier. Name, sex, birth year and breed must match for a renewal candidate. ZIP is evidence rather than an absolute requirement: a renewal can link across ZIPs if its timing fits a narrower window. These assumptions do not prove that two licenses describe the same dog.

First, keep one copy of licenses with identical prepared identity fields and license dates. In this saved snapshot, the 793 additional copies also have identical values in all eight original source columns. Keep the first source row for each repeated record.

```{r}
#| label: remove-repeated-license-records
licenses_with_matching_names |>
  distinct(name, sex, birth_year, breed, zipcode,
           license_issue_date, license_expiry_date, .keep_all = TRUE) ->
  licenses_unique
```

### Put two licenses side by side
Prepare the fields needed to compare licenses, keeping their existing names. Use the same records for both sides, called A and B. These letters identify the sides of the comparison; they do not yet say which license was issued first. `license_records_b <- license_records_a` gives B the whole table held in A, not a single record. Both sides contain the same licenses; nothing is saved to disk.

```{r}
#| label: prepare-license-pair-columns
licenses_unique |>
  select(name, sex, birth_year, breed,
         source_row_id, zipcode,
         license_issue_date, license_expiry_date) ->
  license_records_a

license_records_b <- license_records_a
```

For the walkthrough, follow two actual DEXTER licenses through these steps. The source row numbers select this display example only; they do not restrict the matching pipeline. `print(width = Inf)` shows all selected columns instead of hiding some when the console is narrow.

```{r}
#| label: preview-two-license-records
example_license_rows <- c(19296, 56815)

license_records_a |>
  filter(source_row_id %in% example_license_rows) |>
  select(source_row_id, name, sex, birth_year, breed, zipcode,
         license_issue_date, license_expiry_date) |>
  print(width = Inf)
```

Join records whose name, sex, birth year and breed match. The join keeps these four matching columns once. For the other columns, `suffix = c("_a", "_b")` adds the side to the existing name: for example, `license_issue_date_a` and `license_issue_date_b`. Each license still has both an issue date and an expiry date. ZIP is not a join requirement because a dog may have moved.

```{r}
#| label: pair-matching-licenses
license_records_a |>
  inner_join(
    license_records_b,
    by = c("name", "sex", "birth_year", "breed"),
    suffix = c("_a", "_b"),
    relationship = "many-to-many"
  ) ->
  license_pairs
```

An inner join keeps every matching combination. `relationship = "many-to-many"` acknowledges that several licenses on either side can share these fields. The pairs are candidates for comparison, not established matches to the same dog.

These two records produce four combinations: each record with itself, and the two directions of the comparison. Show their source rows and issue dates side by side.

```{r}
#| label: preview-license-pair-combinations
license_pairs |>
  filter(source_row_id_a %in% example_license_rows,
         source_row_id_b %in% example_license_rows) |>
  select(source_row_id_a, source_row_id_b,
         license_issue_date_a, license_issue_date_b) |>
  print(width = Inf)
```

### Put each pair in date order
Keep pairs where license B was issued after license A. This removes self-matches, reverse copies of a pair and same-day pairs. It establishes the direction of the comparison; the renewal and correction rules below decide whether a pair qualifies for linking.

```{r}
#| label: order-license-pairs
license_pairs |>
  filter(license_issue_date_b > license_issue_date_a) ->
  license_pairs_in_date_order
```

Only the forward comparison remains for these two DEXTER licenses: source row 19296 → 56815. Their expiry dates have not been compared yet.

```{r}
#| label: preview-license-pairs-in-date-order
license_pairs_in_date_order |>
  filter(source_row_id_a %in% example_license_rows,
         source_row_id_b %in% example_license_rows) |>
  select(source_row_id_a, source_row_id_b,
         license_issue_date_a, license_issue_date_b) |>
  print(width = Inf)
```

### Subtract the license dates
Subtract license A’s expiry date from license B’s issue date to measure the gap or overlap. Separately, subtract A’s issue date from B’s issue date to measure how close together the licenses were issued.

```{r}
#| label: subtract-license-dates
license_pairs_in_date_order |>
  mutate(
    time_from_expiry = license_issue_date_b - license_expiry_date_a,
    time_between_issues = license_issue_date_b - license_issue_date_a
  ) ->
  license_time_differences
```

R gives these differences a time-difference type. Convert them to numeric days so we can compare them with the day windows below. `as.numeric()` is a type conversion; `units = "days"` tells it which unit to use. Without that argument a date-time difference may be expressed in seconds. Negative `days_from_expiry` means overlap; positive means a gap.

```{r}
#| label: express-license-gaps-in-days
license_time_differences |>
  mutate(
    days_from_expiry = as.numeric(time_from_expiry, units = "days"),
    days_between_issues = as.numeric(time_between_issues, units = "days")
  ) |>
  select(-time_from_expiry, -time_between_issues) ->
  license_date_gaps
```

For the same DEXTER pair, B was issued four days before A expired, so the expiry difference is −4 days. Their issue dates are 377 days apart. These answer different questions: proximity to expiry suggests a renewal, while proximity between issue dates can suggest a correction.

```{r}
#| label: preview-license-date-gaps
license_date_gaps |>
  filter(source_row_id_a %in% example_license_rows,
         source_row_id_b %in% example_license_rows) |>
  select(license_issue_date_a, license_expiry_date_a,
         license_issue_date_b, license_expiry_date_b,
         days_from_expiry, days_between_issues) |>
  print(width = Inf)
```

### See the license periods overlap
Each line runs from the recorded issue date (circle) to the expiry date (triangle). These are the same two DEXTER records shown above. This display does not decide whether they belong to one dog.

```{r}
#| label: plot-example-license-periods
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3
license_records_a |>
  filter(source_row_id %in% example_license_rows) |>
  mutate(license = case_when(
    source_row_id == 19296 ~ "License A",
    source_row_id == 56815 ~ "License B"
  )) ->
  example_license_periods

license_timeline <- ggplot(example_license_periods, aes(y = license, color = license)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = license_issue_date, xend = license_expiry_date,
                   yend = license), linewidth = 2) +
  geom_point(aes(x = license_issue_date), shape = 16, size = 3) +
  geom_point(aes(x = license_expiry_date), shape = 17, size = 3) +
  scale_y_discrete(limits = c("License B", "License A")) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("License A" = "#007C83", "License B" = "#B35C00")) +
  labs(x = "Recorded license date", y = NULL,
       title = "DEXTER: two recorded license periods",
       caption = "Circle = issued; triangle = expires. Both licenses record ZIP 10467.") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

license_timeline
```

The overlap is short compared with the full license periods. Zoom into January 2024 to see it: B begins on January 17, while A does not expire until January 21. Both lines cover those four days. B’s issue date minus A’s expiry date is therefore −4 days. A positive difference would mean B starts after A ends, leaving a gap; zero means the two dates coincide.

```{r}
#| label: plot-example-license-overlap
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3
# These limits zoom the example display; they do not filter the license data.
example_zoom_dates <- ymd(c("2024-01-12", "2024-01-26"), tz = "UTC")

license_timeline +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = example_zoom_dates) +
  scale_x_datetime(date_breaks = "2 days", date_labels = "%b %d") +
  labs(title = "Close-up: B starts four days before A expires",
       caption = "January 17–21: overlapping license periods. The lines continue beyond this close-up.")
```

### Consolidate likely license-term changes
Some licenses are reissued shortly afterward with the same expiry month and day but a later expiry year. Treat these as likely term changes before looking for renewals. Name, sex, birth year and breed already match. Also require the same ZIP and issue dates no more than fourteen days apart. Fourteen days is a judgment call, not a proven boundary. Unknown breeds provide weaker identifying evidence.

```{r}
#| label: find-likely-license-term-changes
term_change_window_days <- 14

license_date_gaps |>
  mutate(
    expiry_month_a = month(license_expiry_date_a),
    expiry_month_b = month(license_expiry_date_b),
    expiry_day_a = day(license_expiry_date_a),
    expiry_day_b = day(license_expiry_date_b),
    expiry_year_a = year(license_expiry_date_a),
    expiry_year_b = year(license_expiry_date_b)
  ) |>
  filter(zipcode_a == zipcode_b,
         days_between_issues <= term_change_window_days,
         expiry_month_a == expiry_month_b,
         expiry_day_a == expiry_day_b,
         expiry_year_b > expiry_year_a) ->
  possible_term_changes
```

Keep only term-change links with one possible replacement in each direction. This applies the competition check to term changes themselves, before ordinary renewals can introduce competing links.

```{r}
#| label: keep-unambiguous-license-term-changes
possible_term_changes |>
  group_by(source_row_id_a) |>
  mutate(possible_replacements = n()) |>
  ungroup() |>
  group_by(source_row_id_b) |>
  mutate(possible_originals = n()) |>
  ungroup() |>
  filter(possible_replacements == 1, possible_originals == 1) ->
  accepted_term_changes
```

In this snapshot, this finds 62 separate pairs. For SCOOPER, the December 19, 2023 license expires January 13, 2027; the January 1, 2024 license extends expiry to January 13, 2029. Retain the January 1 license for renewal matching. That leaves one candidate renewal of the older SCOOPER license instead of two competing candidates. ALMA has the same pattern with issues ten days apart.

```{r}
#| label: preview-license-term-changes
accepted_term_changes |>
  filter(name %in% c("SCOOPER", "ALMA")) |>
  select(name, source_row_id_a, source_row_id_b,
         license_issue_date_a, license_issue_date_b,
         license_expiry_date_a, license_expiry_date_b) |>
  print(width = Inf)
```

Remove the replaced licenses from subsequent comparisons. Keep the term-change links so those source records can later receive the same dog group as their replacements. This does not discard their source correspondence.

```{r}
#| label: use-replacement-licenses-for-renewals
replaced_license_rows <- accepted_term_changes$source_row_id_a

license_date_gaps |>
  filter(!source_row_id_a %in% replaced_license_rows,
         !source_row_id_b %in% replaced_license_rows) ->
  license_pairs_after_term_changes
```

### Choose the renewal window for each pair
The chosen settings are 30 days on either side of expiry within a ZIP, seven days across ZIPs, and five days between issues for a possible expiry correction. They are practical assumptions, not proof of identity. The [sensitivity appendix](appendices/license-consolidation-sensitivity.qmd) compares alternatives without changing this preparation run.

```{r}
#| label: set-license-windows
renewal_window_days <- 30
moving_window_days <- 7
correction_window_days <- 5

license_pairs_after_term_changes |>
  mutate(same_zipcode = zipcode_a == zipcode_b) ->
  license_zip_comparison

license_zip_comparison |>
  mutate(allowed_renewal_gap_days = case_when(
    same_zipcode ~ renewal_window_days,
    .default = moving_window_days
  )) ->
  license_pairs_with_windows
```

Read `condition ~ result` as “if this condition matches, use this result.” Here, a matching ZIP gets 30 days; otherwise use seven. The setting and the resulting column have different names.

### Identify possible renewals
License B was issued after license A because of the date-order filter. A renewal also needs B to expire after A and a gap within the selected window. `case_when()` checks each condition in order: these first three cases rule a pair out; otherwise it qualifies. TRUE and FALSE are the answers to that decision, not replacement dates.

```{r}
#| label: identify-possible-renewals
license_pairs_with_windows |>
  mutate(possible_renewal = case_when(
    license_expiry_date_b <= license_expiry_date_a ~ FALSE,
    days_from_expiry < -allowed_renewal_gap_days ~ FALSE,
    days_from_expiry > allowed_renewal_gap_days ~ FALSE,
    .default = TRUE
  )) ->
  license_renewal_decisions
```

### Identify possible expiry corrections
A possible correction needs the same ZIP, issues no more than five days apart, and a changed expiry. Name, sex, birth year and breed already match because they were join fields. A correction can shorten or lengthen the period; we do not change identity fields or combine different names.

```{r}
#| label: identify-possible-expiry-corrections
license_renewal_decisions |>
  mutate(possible_correction = case_when(
    !same_zipcode ~ FALSE,
    days_between_issues > correction_window_days ~ FALSE,
    license_expiry_date_b == license_expiry_date_a ~ FALSE,
    .default = TRUE
  )) ->
  license_pair_decisions
```

Keep pairs satisfying either rule. The `|` means “or.” Assign a reason for inspection; where a pair qualifies as both, the renewal description takes precedence.

```{r}
#| label: keep-candidate-license-links
license_pair_decisions |>
  filter(possible_renewal | possible_correction) ->
  candidate_links

candidate_links |>
  mutate(link_reason = case_when(
    possible_renewal & same_zipcode ~ "renewal in same ZIP",
    possible_renewal ~ "renewal across ZIPs",
    .default = "possible expiry correction"
  )) ->
  candidate_links_with_reasons
```

### Count competing continuations
For each license on side A, count how many licenses on side B could continue it. `n()` counts rows in the group; `mutate()` puts that count beside each candidate pair. `ungroup()` ends this grouping before we count in the other direction.

```{r}
#| label: count-possible-license-successors
candidate_links_with_reasons |>
  group_by(source_row_id_a) |>
  mutate(possible_successors = n()) |>
  ungroup() ->
  links_with_successor_counts
```

For each license on side B, count how many licenses on side A could precede it:

```{r}
#| label: count-possible-license-predecessors
links_with_successor_counts |>
  group_by(source_row_id_b) |>
  mutate(possible_predecessors = n()) |>
  ungroup() ->
  links_with_both_counts
```

For example, A → D and B → D give D two possible predecessors. We leave both links unresolved. C → E can be accepted if neither C nor E has another candidate in the relevant direction.

```{r}
#| label: decide-unambiguous-license-links
links_with_both_counts |>
  mutate(link_accepted = case_when(
    possible_successors > 1 ~ FALSE,
    possible_predecessors > 1 ~ FALSE,
    .default = TRUE
  )) ->
  license_links

license_links |>
  filter(link_accepted) |>
  arrange(license_issue_date_b, source_row_id_b) ->
  accepted_license_links
```

The rejected links remain in `license_links` for inspection. They are not proof of different dogs; they are cases where this rule cannot choose a unique match.

### Record where each license gets its group
For an accepted renewal, license B receives license A’s group. For a term change, the replaced license A receives its replacement B’s group. Keep both instructions in a table: `source_row_id` is the license receiving the group; `group_source_row` identifies the license supplying it. These are source-record numbers, not ZIP codes.

```{r}
#| label: record-license-group-assignments
accepted_license_links |>
  select(group_source_row = source_row_id_a,
         source_row_id = source_row_id_b) ->
  renewal_assignments

accepted_term_changes |>
  select(group_source_row = source_row_id_b,
         source_row_id = source_row_id_a) ->
  replacement_assignments

bind_rows(renewal_assignments, replacement_assignments) ->
  group_assignments
```

`bind_rows()` stacks the two sets of instructions. Follow SCOOPER’s three source records in the displays below: the revised renewal 54311 takes the original license 5954’s group, and the replaced renewal 52219 takes 54311’s group.

```{r}
#| label: preview-scooper-group-assignments
scooper_source_rows <- c(5954, 52219, 54311)

group_assignments |>
  filter(source_row_id %in% scooper_source_rows)
```

### Start with one group per license
Initially each license’s group is its own source-row number. The number is a bookkeeping label for an estimated dog, not a verified dog identifier.

```{r}
#| label: start-license-groups
licenses_unique |>
  select(source_row_id) |>
  mutate(license_group = source_row_id) ->
  license_groups_table

license_groups_table |>
  filter(source_row_id %in% scooper_source_rows)
```

### Look up the proposed groups
Look up the current group of the license supplying each assignment. The left join keeps every assignment and matches its `group_source_row` against the group table’s `source_row_id`.

```{r}
#| label: look-up-license-group-updates
group_assignments |>
  left_join(license_groups_table,
            by = c("group_source_row" = "source_row_id")) |>
  select(source_row_id, proposed_group = license_group) ->
  group_updates

group_updates |>
  filter(source_row_id %in% scooper_source_rows)
```

### Apply one round of updates
Attach the proposed groups to the full table. This left join retains every license, including those with no assignment. When there is no proposed group, keep the existing group; otherwise use the proposed value. Display the old and next groups together before replacing the working table.

```{r}
#| label: apply-one-license-group-round
license_groups_table |>
  left_join(group_updates, by = "source_row_id") |>
  mutate(next_group = case_when(
    is.na(proposed_group) ~ license_group,
    .default = proposed_group
  )) ->
  groups_reviewed

groups_reviewed |>
  filter(source_row_id %in% scooper_source_rows) |>
  select(source_row_id, license_group, proposed_group, next_group)
```

Count the changed assignments, then use the next groups as the working table. This count controls repetition; it is not a data-quality guard.

```{r}
#| label: keep-updated-license-groups
groups_reviewed |>
  summarise(changed_records = sum(next_group != license_group)) ->
  group_change_count

changed_records <- group_change_count$changed_records

groups_reviewed |>
  select(source_row_id, license_group = next_group) ->
  license_groups_table
```

### Repeat until the groups stop changing
One round moves group numbers one connection along. SCOOPER’s revised renewal receives group 5954 in the first round, but its replaced renewal needs a second round to receive that group. Repeat the same lookups and updates until no assignments change. `while` means “repeat this block while the condition is true.” The loop is an additional programming construct; the transformations inside are the table operations shown above.

```{r}
#| label: repeat-license-group-updates
while (changed_records > 0) {
  group_assignments |>
    left_join(license_groups_table,
              by = c("group_source_row" = "source_row_id")) |>
    select(source_row_id, proposed_group = license_group) ->
    group_updates

  license_groups_table |>
    left_join(group_updates, by = "source_row_id") |>
    mutate(next_group = case_when(
      is.na(proposed_group) ~ license_group,
      .default = proposed_group
    )) ->
    groups_reviewed

  groups_reviewed |>
    summarise(changed_records = sum(next_group != license_group)) ->
    group_change_count

  changed_records <- group_change_count$changed_records

  groups_reviewed |>
    select(source_row_id, license_group = next_group) ->
    license_groups_table
}

license_groups_table |>
  filter(source_row_id %in% scooper_source_rows)
```

Attach the completed group table to the original distinct licenses. This includes replaced licenses, so we can recover their recorded fields and trace every source record without returning them to renewal matching.

```{r}
#| label: attach-license-groups
licenses_unique |>
  left_join(license_groups_table, by = "source_row_id") ->
  licenses_grouped
```

### Keep the earliest observed license in each group
Use the earliest observed license to supply the dog’s ZIP and other recorded fields. We are interested in location around naming, so the earliest available location is a more relevant proxy than the most recent one. It is not necessarily the dog’s first license or where it was named: this single extract can omit earlier records, and ownership may have changed. Neighborhood income also does not establish the owner’s income.

Term-change matching still uses the revised license’s dates. Once the group is established, this selection considers all its source licenses, including the replaced records. In this snapshot there are no tied earliest issue dates among the distinct licenses in a group. Unlinked licenses remain separate estimates; mistaken merges and missed renewals remain possible.

```{r}
#| label: estimate-individual-dogs
licenses_grouped |>
  group_by(license_group) |>
  slice_min(order_by = license_issue_date, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup() ->
  dogs_consolidated
```

Keep a separate in-memory correspondence table so every eligible source license, including repeated copies, can be traced to its assigned group:

```{r}
#| label: record-license-membership
licenses_grouped |>
  select(name, sex, birth_year, breed, zipcode,
         license_issue_date, license_expiry_date, license_group) ->
  unique_license_groups

licenses_with_matching_names |>
  left_join(unique_license_groups,
            by = c("name", "sex", "birth_year", "breed", "zipcode",
                   "license_issue_date", "license_expiry_date")) |>
  select(source_row_id, license_group) ->
  license_membership
```

The left join preserves every eligible source row. Its matching fields identify the unique prepared license created above. Group numbers and decision fields stay out of `dogs_prepared`; no CSV is written.

## Keep the dog fields

Keep name and ZIP for matching, and sex, birth year and breed for possible further comparisons. The source row number links each dog to its recorded values. Leave the extract year, license dates and report fields out of this analysis table.

```{r}
#| label: select-dog-fields
dogs_consolidated |>
  select(source_row_id, name, sex, birth_year, breed, zipcode) ->
  dogs_prepared

dogs_prepared |>
  preview()
```

## Cleaning summary

### Effect of consolidating licenses

Compare the number of eligible licenses with the number of estimated dogs. The difference counts additional license records consolidated, not dogs excluded. `nrow()` counts table rows; no per-dog license-count column is needed.

```{r}
#| label: summarize-license-consolidation
licenses_with_matching_names |>
  nrow() ->
  eligible_license_count

dogs_prepared |>
  nrow() ->
  estimated_dog_count

tibble(
  eligible_license_records = eligible_license_count,
  estimated_dogs = estimated_dog_count,
  additional_license_records_consolidated = eligible_license_count - estimated_dog_count
) ->
  consolidation_summary

consolidation_summary
```

### Missing names overall

Add the earlier per-ZIP counts to report missing names across all source licenses. Divide the missing-name count by the source-license count to get the overall share. The six missing-name labels are counted together.

```{r}
#| label: summarize-missing-names-overall
missing_by_zip |>
  summarise(
    source_license_records = sum(source_license_records),
    missing_name_records = sum(missing_name_records),
    missing_name_share = missing_name_records / source_license_records
  )
```

### Unknown breeds and compound names

Count these characteristics among the estimated dogs, using each dog's retained license. Each `sum()` counts TRUE answers in the report fields recorded before formatting names. These counts describe the prepared dogs; they do not exclude any dogs.

```{r}
#| label: summarize-dog-characteristics
dogs_consolidated |>
  summarise(
    dogs_with_unknown_breed = sum(breed_unknown),
    dogs_with_compound_names = sum(compound_name)
  )
```

Different dogs can share identifying fields, and a dog's recorded details can change. These remain estimates of individual dogs, with alternative assumptions compared in the appendix.


## Why keep a sensitivity appendix?
Sixteen licenses record TEDDY, male, born in 2022, Shih Tzu Crossbreed. Our chosen renewal windows give 14 estimated dogs. Wider windows can reveal competing matches: 60/14-day windows leave 16 estimates, while 90/30-day windows give 14 by accepting different links. The five-day correction setting does not affect this example.

Timing is a useful heuristic, not a dog identifier. These differences show how the estimate depends on our assumptions; they do not establish the true number of dogs or a confidence interval. The [sensitivity appendix](appendices/license-consolidation-sensitivity.qmd) contains the alternative runs, possible-correction inspection and aligned license timelines for discussion. They are separate from this notebook’s single preparation rule.
